q: On moving down a group of the periodic table, atomic radius generally:
o: Increases, because a new electron shell is added in each period
Stays the same, because the outer configuration is the same
x: Each step down a group adds a new shell, so the outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and the atom is larger, despite the higher nuclear charge.

q: The s-block of the periodic table consists of:
o: Groups I and II (alkali and alkaline earth metals)
x: In s-block elements the last electron enters an s orbital; these are Groups I and II. Groups 13 to 18 form the p-block, groups 3 to 12 the d-block.

q: Atomic radius decreases from left to right across a period mainly because:
o: A new shell is added for each element
Shielding by inner electrons increases sharply
Nuclear charge increases while electrons are added to the same shell
Atomic mass increases across the period
x: Across a period the proton number rises but the electrons go into the same shell, with little extra shielding. The stronger pull draws the shell closer.

q: An element has the configuration [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p³. It belongs to the:
x: The block is set by the subshell receiving the last electron. Here the last electrons enter 4p, so it is a p-block element (arsenic, Group V).

q: Which comparison of radii is correct?
x: Adding an electron increases repulsion and expands the electron cloud, so an anion is larger than its atom. A cation is smaller than its atom.

q: In the f-block elements, the last electron enters:
x: The f-block (lanthanides and actinides) fills the 4f and 5f subshells. The (n−1)d subshell is filled in the d-block.

q: O²⁻, F⁻, Na⁺ and Mg²⁺ all have 10 electrons. Which of these ions is the smallest?
x: In an isoelectronic series the ion with the most protons pulls the same 10 electrons in most strongly. Mg²⁺ has 12 protons, the most here, so it is smallest; O²⁻ (8 protons) is largest.

q: In the d-block (transition) elements, the last electron enters the:
x: In the fourth period, for example, the 3d subshell fills after 4s, so the differentiating electron goes into the (n−1)d subshell.

q: The Cl–Cl bond length in a chlorine molecule is 198 pm. The covalent radius of chlorine is:
x: Covalent radius is half the distance between the nuclei of two identical atoms joined by a single covalent bond: 198/2 = 99 pm.

q: The element with atomic number 20 is in:
x: Z = 20 is calcium, 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s². The last electron is in 4s, so it is in the s-block, period 4, Group II.

q: Which equation represents the first ionisation energy of sodium?
x: Ionisation energy is the energy to remove one electron from each atom in one mole of isolated gaseous atoms. Starting from the solid adds atomisation; adding an electron is electron affinity.

q: The element with atomic number 26 is in:
x: Z = 26 is iron, [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s². Its outermost shell is n = 4 and the last electron enters 3d, so it is a d-block element of period 4.

q: The first ionisation energy of magnesium is higher than that of aluminium because:
o: Aluminium has a smaller nuclear charge than magnesium
Magnesium has more electron shells than aluminium
The electron removed from aluminium is a 3p electron, higher in energy and more shielded than magnesium's 3s electron
The electron removed from magnesium is a 3p electron
x: Mg is [Ne]3s² and Al is [Ne]3s²3p¹. The single 3p electron of Al is higher in energy and partly shielded by the 3s pair, so it is removed more easily.

q: The element with atomic number 35 belongs to:
x: Z = 35 is bromine, [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p⁵. Seven outer electrons (4s² 4p⁵) give Group VIIA, the n = 4 shell gives period 4, and the last electron in 4p gives the p-block.

q: The second ionisation energy of sodium is much greater than its first because the second electron:
o: Is removed from the same 3s orbital as the first electron
Is added to the atom rather than removed
Is removed from a filled inner shell, closer to the nucleus, and from a positive ion
Is removed from a larger, neutral atom
x: Na is [Ne]3s¹. After the 3s electron goes, the next one must come from the full 2p subshell of Na⁺, which is much closer to the nucleus and held strongly.

q: The general outer electronic configuration of p-block elements is:
x: p-block elements have a filled ns subshell and one to six electrons in np. ns¹⁻² is the s-block and the d and f patterns are the other blocks.

q: Which element has the most negative (highest) electron affinity?
x: Chlorine releases the most energy on gaining an electron. Fluorine's value is a little lower because its very small 2p shell causes strong repulsion with the incoming electron.

q: The modern periodic law states that the properties of elements are a periodic function of their:
x: After Moseley's work the table is arranged by atomic number (proton number), and properties repeat periodically with it. Mendeleev's original law used atomic masses, the tempting older answer.

q: The third shell (n = 3) can hold 18 electrons, yet the third period contains only 8 elements. The reason is that:
o: The 4s subshell is lower in energy than 3d, so 3d fills only in the fourth period
The 3d subshell can hold only 8 electrons
The 3p subshell fills after the 4s subshell
x: Period 3 fills 3s and 3p (2 + 6 = 8 electrons). By the Aufbau order 4s comes before 3d, so 3d is filled by the transition elements of period 4. A d subshell holds 10 electrons, not 8.

q: Which pair of atomic numbers belongs to elements of the same group?
x: Z = 12 (Mg, [Ne] 3s²) and Z = 20 (Ca, [Ar] 4s²) both have an ns² outer configuration: Group IIA. 13 (Al, Group IIIA) and 21 (Sc, Group IIIB) share three outer electrons but are in different groups, the tempting slip.

q: What is the ground-state electronic configuration of the element with atomic number 29, and to which block does it belong?
x: Z = 29 is copper; a completely filled 3d¹⁰ subshell is extra stable, so one 4s electron moves into 3d, giving [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹. Its differentiating electrons are 3d, so it is a d-block (transition) element. The Aufbau-only answer 3d⁹ 4s² is the common slip.

q: Which shows the correct order of electronegativity?
x: Across period 2 nuclear charge rises and radius falls, so electronegativity increases from C to F: C 2.5, N 3.0, O 3.5, F 4.0. Fluorine is the most electronegative element; the reversed order follows metallic character, not electronegativity.

q: The first four ionisation energies of an element X are 738, 1451, 7733 and 10 540 kJ mol⁻¹. In which group of the periodic table is X?
x: The large jump is between the 2nd and 3rd ionisation energies (1451 → 7733), so the third electron comes from a filled inner shell. X has 2 valence electrons: Group IIA (this is magnesium). Placing the jump after the first value gives Group IA.

q: Which shows the elements in order of increasing metallic character?
x: Metallic character falls across a period (Na > Mg > Al) and rises down a group (K > Na), because ionisation energy falls as the outer electron is held less tightly. So Al < Mg < Na < K. The reverse list is the order of decreasing metallic character.

q: Which oxide of a period 3 element is amphoteric?
x: Al₂O₃ reacts with acids (to give Al³⁺ salts) and with strong alkalis (to give aluminates), so it is amphoteric. Na₂O and MgO are basic and SO₃ is acidic.

q: Silicon dioxide does not dissolve in water, yet it is classified as an acidic oxide because it:
o: Reacts with dilute HCl to form SiCl₄
Turns blue litmus red when suspended in water
Reacts with hot concentrated NaOH to form sodium silicate
Reacts with water to form a strong acid
x: SiO₂ + 2NaOH → Na₂SiO₃ + H₂O: reaction with a base to give a salt and water shows acidic character. It does not react with dilute acids or with water, so the other choices describe things that do not happen.

q: Which of these period 3 oxides consists of small, separate molecules?
x: SO₃ is a simple molecular (covalent) oxide with weak forces between molecules, so it has a low melting point. MgO and Al₂O₃ are giant ionic lattices and SiO₂ is a giant covalent network; SiO₂ is the tempting covalent choice but is not molecular.

q: Which period 3 chloride dissolves in water to give a neutral solution (pH about 7)?
x: NaCl is ionic and its ions are only hydrated, so the solution is neutral. AlCl₃ gives an acidic solution through hydrolysis of hydrated Al³⁺, and SiCl₄ and PCl₅ are completely hydrolysed to HCl.

q: Phosphorus pentachloride reacts with excess water. The products are:
x: PCl₅ + 4H₂O → H₃PO₄ + 5HCl; phosphorus keeps its +5 oxidation state, so phosphoric(V) acid forms. H₃PO₃ (phosphorus +3) comes from PCl₃, the usual mix-up.

q: When sodium hydride, NaH, is added to water, the products are:
x: NaH is an ionic hydride containing H⁻, which reacts with water: NaH + H₂O → NaOH + H₂. H⁻ (−1) and H in water (+1) combine to give H₂ (0). Na₂O would itself react with water, so it is not a product.

q: Molten sodium hydride, NaH, is electrolysed. Where is hydrogen gas liberated, and why?
o: At the anode, because the hydride ion H⁻ is oxidised
At the cathode, because H⁺ ions are reduced
At the cathode, because Na⁺ is reduced and releases H₂
At the anode, because H⁺ ions are oxidised
x: NaH is ionic, Na⁺H⁻, so hydrogen is present as the negative ion; it moves to the anode and loses electrons: 2H⁻ → H₂ + 2e⁻. Sodium forms at the cathode. Assuming hydrogen is always H⁺ gives the cathode answer.

q: In which compound does the period 3 element show its maximum (group) oxidation number?
x: Cl in Cl₂O₇ is +7, equal to its group number VIIA. In SO₂ sulphur is +4 (maximum +6), in PCl₃ phosphorus is +3 (maximum +5) and in Cl₂O chlorine is only +1.

q: 0.1 mol of SO₃ is dissolved in water. What mass of NaOH is needed to neutralise the solution completely? (NaOH = 40 g mol⁻¹)
x: SO₃ is an acidic oxide: SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄, giving 0.1 mol of a dibasic acid. H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O needs 0.2 mol NaOH = 8.0 g. Treating the acid as monobasic gives 4.0 g.

q: Which list shows period 3 oxides in order from most basic to most acidic?
x: Across period 3 the oxides change from ionic and basic (Na₂O most basic, then MgO) through amphoteric Al₂O₃ to covalent and acidic (SO₃). Putting MgO before Na₂O ignores that basic character falls as metallic character falls.

q: Which hydride of a period 2 element has the highest boiling point?
x: H₂O boils at 100 °C. Each molecule has two O–H hydrogens and two lone pairs, so it forms more hydrogen bonds per molecule than HF (b.p. about 20 °C) or NH₃; CH₄ has none. HF has the strongest single hydrogen bond, which makes it tempting.
